title: I Took the Rolling-Mill Booking to the Intern Who Left My Gauge

parts.text: I stepped into mill one at 12:07 p.m. and intern Beau was already using my numbered gauge. The board said: THIRTY MINUTES. GAUGE STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty, metals lead, holding a clipboard that listed our pass. Beau shrugged. "Interns learn the mill." I photographed the board, the booking, and his sheet in my mill. Then I asked for the mill booking. At 12:15 the metals desk pinged why Beau's sheet sat in our mill. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The metals desk can see Beau's sheet in mill one during our pass.

social.video_title: He left his sheet in my numbered mill — Part 1/2
social.description: Rolling mill, an intern in my mill, a thirty-minute clock he posted. I logged the sheet. Would you have asked for the mill booking?

parts.text: Beau called it anneal passes until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the mill still. The gauge went back to my numbered clip. Beau ran a slot of their own and told the next intern atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: INTERNS DO NOT LEARN ON A BOOKED MILL. I keep our pass on a labeled card. Beau brown-bags his sheets. The mill finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Interns do not learn on a booked mill — Part 2/2
social.description: Mill booking, numbered gauge, and a second line on the board. Were anneal passes ever our mill?
